senses.gloss:
Kṛṣṇa
(also, श्रीकृष्ण)
------------------------------------------
1. Introduction
The philosophy of the उपनिषद्स् is characterized by a rational temper, a passion for the welfare of the human beings and a spirit of harmony as applied to the whole world. This philosophy, though impersonal in itself, has yet been the womb of a galaxy of personalities who have shone brilliantly in the horizon of India. राम and कृष्ण are the brightest of these स्तर्स्; and, they have dominated the pages of Indian cultural history for centuries. Not only that, they have become models for emulation for later ages.
Between the two, it is perhaps, कृष्ण who has influenced the Indian thought, life and culture in a more profound way. He has entered, not only into its religion and philosophy, but also into its म्य्स्तिचिस्म् and poetry, painting and sculpture, मुसिच् and dancing, and all aspects of the Indian folklore. To say the least, he has mesmerized a whole people for generations. Where else can one seek for the secret of this mesmerism of कृष्ण except in his great character and noble life?
And yet, it is a strange irony that no other person in India’s history and culture has been subjected to so much of unsympathetic or even foul criticism, based on either an incomplete or an incorrect understanding of all the facts available, if not a deliberate distortion of the same to serve an ulterior purpose. True, there have also been presentations of his personality by over-enthusiastic votaries that rob quite a bit of the grace of a wondrously graceful personality. Hence an attempt will be made here to steer clear of the extremes and give a fairly balanced assessment of his life, personality and work.
2. Several Kṛṣṇas
We come across several Kṛṣṇas in the Hindu scriptures. The Ṛgveda (1.116.23) mentions one कृष्ण, the ड़थेर् of a Viśvakāya. The last मण्डल or section of the same work (10.42-44) attributes two sūktas or hymns to the sage कृष्ण. We meet with a कृष्ण Āṅgirasa in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (30.9) and a कृष्ण हारीत in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (3.26). Then there is कृष्ण द्वैपायन, also called व्यास, the reputed author of the epic Mahābhārata. It can safely be assumed that none of these Kṛṣṇas is the कृष्ण of our study.
However, the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.17.6) mentions कृष्ण-Devakīputra as a disciple of घोर आङ्गिरस by whom he was taught the science of Puruṣayajña. It is very likely that this is the same as कृष्ण, the son of Vasudeva and देवकी. The only snag is that सान्दीपनि has been specifically mentioned as the गुरु or preceptor of कृष्ण and not घोर आङ्गिरस. सान्दीपनि belonged to the अङ्गिरस् गोत्र (i.e., that he was a descendant of the sage अङ्गिरस्). The title `ghora' (`the terrible') may be explained as indicating that he was a strict disciplinarian.">1
Some scholars opine that the कृष्ण we worship today is a syncretic deity of four personalities: विष्णु (a solar deity), नारायण (of some theistic philosophical systems), वासुदेव (of the भागवत cult) and Gopāla (a cowherd king of Ābhīra). However, this much has to be conceded that at the time of the epic story of the Mahābhārata, कृष्ण was already well-known, considered not only as a very great person, but, even deserving worship as a manifestation of the Divine.
3. Date of Kṛṣṇa
Since कृष्ण took an active part in the महाभारत war, his date naturally depends upon the date of this war. Scholars have been battling for decades to fix its date. Adopting various methods like philological considerations of the language of the epic, or, allowing an average length of period of a ruler and calculating backwards from the time of a known ruler whose date has been fixed, the European scholars 2 have generally assigned it to the period 1400—300 B. C. Indian scholars, 3 who have seriously weighed the internal astronomical evidence, have concluded that the latest date can be around 1400 B. C. They are more inclined, however, to accept the period 3200 to 3100 B. C.
4. Sources of the कृष्ण Story
The primary sources of the कृष्ण story are four: the Mahābhārata, and its adjunct Harivaṁśa, the Viṣṇupurāṇa and the Bhāgavata. The story is also met with in other पुराणस् like the Brahmapurāṇa, Padmapurāṇa and Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa (Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa).
In the Mahābhārata, कृष्ण appears for the first time during the मर्रिअगे of द्रौपदी with the Pāṇḍavas. Though there are casual references to his earlier life, no details have been given. To make up for this lacuna, as it were, the Hari-vaṁśa was added as an adjunct, later. It is a fairly long work of over 16,000 verses and deals with the story of कृष्ण in great detail in the section called Viṣṇuparva. The Viṣṇupurāṇa (A. D. 300; 6000 verses) is one of the earliest पुराणस् and deals with the story of कृष्ण in the fifth section (pañcamāṁśa). The Bhāgavata (A. D. 600; 18,000 verses) seems to be an expanded version of the Viṣṇupurāṇa in that it deals with practically the same topics, but in much greater detail.
5. Story of कृष्ण in brief
The story of कृष्ण may now be stated briefly, following the accounts given in the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata.
Mother Earth, unable to bear the burden of sins committed by evil kings and rulers, of whom कṁस of मथुरा and जरासन्ध of Magadha were the worst, appealed to ब्रह्मा, the Creator for help. ब्रह्मा prayed to the Supreme Lord नारायण and got the assurance that He would soon be born in this world to eliminate all the evil doers.
Ugrasena of the Yādava race, was the ruler of the kingdom of मथुरा, with its capital at the city of मथुरा. His son कṁस, the crown prince, was a tyrant, dreaded by all and it was he that was practically ruling the kingdom. When देवकी, a daughter of Devaka, the cousin of Ugrasena, came of age, she was married to Vasudeva, the son of शूरसेन, another Yādava chieftain. कṁस who loved his sister देवकी, took the couple out for a ride on a royal chariot, driving it himself. A voice from the void (ākāśa-vāṇī) warned him that the eighth issue of the couple would destroy him. Enraged and unnerved by this quirk of fate, कṁस was about to kill देवकी. Vasudeva intervened and averted the tragedy to his wife, by promising to hand over all the children born of her. Though कṁस spared देवकी’s life, not being prepared to take chances, he put the couple in prison.
Vasudeva kept up his word. कṁस mercilessly slaughtered the first six sons of देवकी. The seventh foetus was mysteriously transferred to the womb of रोहिणी, the elder wife of Vasudeva, now living at गोकुल, a cowherd settlement, across the river यमुना. She gave birth to a hefty boy. Then the Lord entered into देवकी and she conceived for the eighth time. Now she shone with a brilliance that was matchless but soothing. Ever since कṁस came to know of it, he started living in mortal fear. On the blessed day when nature was at its best to welcome the Lord, He appeared to the couple in all His glory and instructed Vasudeva to exchange him for the baby-girl just born to यशोदा, wife of the cowherd chief नन्द, at गोकुल. Then He assumed the form of an extremely charming human baby. The instructions were carried out faithfully. Under the divine spell, the gates of the prison opened up, the guards slept and the river यमुना made way for the transportation of the divine infant.
When कṁस arrived at the prison next morning on hearing the news, he found a baby-girl in his sister’s lap! Since fear of death had dehumanized him, he dashed the babe against a boulder. But, it escaped, flew up into the sky, assumed the fierce form of योगमाया (Durgā) and prophesied that his enemy was living elsewhere and would soon kill him.
The divine child started growing at गोकुल giving the greatest joy to one and all by his bewitching beauty and supremely charming pranks. All attempts of कṁस to kill the child were set at nought by the little fellow who dispatched demon after demon to the abode of death.
Garga, the family priest of the Yādavas arrived at गोकुल and secretly performed the नामकरण (the ritual of christening) for the two children. रोहिणी’s son was christened as राम or बलराम and यशोदा’s baby-son as कृष्ण.
The exploits of कृष्ण at the cowherd settlement included revealing the whole universe in his little mouth to his मोथेर् यशोदा and felling the twin trees by dragging the grinding stone to which he had been tied, in between them. Meanwhile, the elders of the village decided to abandon गोकुल and migrate to Vṛndā-vana, a nearby place, which offered better facilities for a new settlement. It proved to be very attractive to the brothers बलराम and कृष्ण.
Apart from extirpating some more emissaries of death dispatched by कṁस, कृष्ण’s adventures at Vṛndāvana included subduing and driving away the serpent Kāliya from the river to the sea, lifting the गोवर्धन hill up with his little finger and holding it like an umbrella to protect the people of Vṛndāvana from the torrential rain caused by इन्द्र (the king of gods in हेअवेन्) who had been annoyed by कृष्ण’s stopping of worship to him, the Rāsa dance with the गोपीस् on the banks of यमुना and rescuing his foster-ड़थेर् नन्द from drowning.
Finding that all his efforts to assassinate the two children were in vain, कṁस decided to get them to his capital on the pretext of a royal invitation and contrived to kill them there. Accordingly he sent Akrūra, a Yādava chief, with a chariot to Vṛndāvana to bring the two brothers. बलराम and कृष्ण seized this opportunity and went there gladly. After a few more bouts of adventure in the capital and in the palace, कृष्ण killed कṁस, freed his parents Vasudeva and देवकी, as also his grandfather Ugrasena who was then re-installed on the throne.
Vasudeva, then, arranged for the उपनयन (a religious sacrament done at the commencement of Vedic studies) and एदुचतिओन् of the boys under the preceptor सान्दीपनि, living at Avantīpura. The geniuses that they were, बलराम and कृष्ण mastered the well-known sixty-four sciences and arts in just sixty-four days. They returned to मथुरा after restoring to the preceptor his dead son at his request, as गुरुदक्षिणा (respectful offering to the preceptor as a mark of gratitude).
Jarāsandha, the emperor of Magadha, started invading मथुरा with his huge army. Though beaten back, he was returning again and again. So, कृष्ण built an impregnable capital द्वारका in an island in the sea and shifted the people there.
Soon after this, बलराम and कृष्ण married Revatī and रुक्मिणी, the daughters of Revata and Bhīṣmaka. कृष्ण also married Jāmbavatī, the daughter of जाम्बवान्, and, सत्यभामा, the daughter of Satrājit.
Narakāsura, the demon king of Prāg-jyotiṣapura, had abducted and imprisoned 16,000 princesses. कृष्ण invaded his kingdom, killed him in the battle, released the girls and married them, since they had nowhere else to go.
Vasudeva had a sister, Pṛthā by name—but more well-known as Kuntī—who had been married to prince पाण्डु, the ruler of हस्तिनापुर. He died early, leaving five young sons (later known as the Pāṇḍavas) to the care of कुन्ती. She took refuge in भीष्म, the grandsire of the कुरु race, who brought them up along with the hundred Kauravas, sons of the blind king धृतराष्ट्र, the elder brother of पाण्डु. Jealousy and enmity of the Kauravas towards the Pāṇḍavas forced the latter to go into exile. After many a travail, they reached Kāmpilya, the capital of southern Pāñcāla kingdom ruled by Drupada, just in time for the स्वयṁवर (marriage by self-choice) of his daughter द्रौपदी. Disguised as ब्राह्मणस् they too were sitting in the assembly.
Kṛṣṇa also had come there along with बलराम. He immediately recognized the Pāṇḍavas. After the failure of all the princes, अर्जुन, the third of the Pāṇḍava brothers, succeeded in piercing the fish fixed on a special contrivance called matsya-यन्त्र, thus passing the prescribed test. That a beggarly ब्राह्मण succeeded where mighty princes failed, naturally roused the wrath of the kings assembled there. When they started a fight with the Pāṇḍavas, कृष्ण intervened, reminding them all that अर्जुन had won the hand of द्रौपदी according to धर्म or righteous and just way. This cooled their frayed tempers and an ugly situation was averted.
Once, while on a पिल्ग्रिमगे, अर्जुन came to द्वारका and fell in love with सुभद्रा, the sister of कृष्ण. Since the love was mutual and since अर्जुन was the best match for her, कृष्ण successfully contrived to get them married.
When the Pāṇḍavas got their share of half the kingdom, and wanted to build the capital, it was कृष्ण who helped them to clear the Khāṇḍava forest and establish their capital there. It came to be known as इन्द्रप्रस्थ or Khāṇḍavaprastha.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas wanted to perform the राजसूय sacrifice. कृष्ण encouraged him to undertake this ambitious venture. Since the performer of the राजसूय sacrifice would be proclaimed as the emperor, all opposition had to be overcome before taking it up.
Jarāsandha of Magadha was a mighty king and a tyrant. He had to be conquered first, as a part of that victory expedition. कृष्ण, along with अर्जुन and the mighty भीम (the second of the Pāṇḍavas), went to the capital of जरासन्ध in disguise, challenged him to a dual with भीम and got him killed. He then crowned जरासन्ध’s son सहदेव as the king of Magadha. He also released from prison the large number of princes and kings held captive by जरासन्ध.
The राजसूय went off on a grand scale. When the question of who should be offered the ‘agrapūjā’—worship offered to the best of the assembled men, the highest honour bestowed on such occasions—came up, there was near unanimity in favour of कृष्ण. The lone dissenter was शिशुपाल, the king of Cedi, who did so, out of an old enmity. Since he abused कृष्ण, भीम and others in that august assembly and even challenged them to fight him, कृष्ण was obliged to kill him using his celebrated discus, the सुदर्शन.
Unable to bear the prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas, दुर्योधन, the eldest of the Kauravas challenged युधिष्ठिर, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, to गम्ब्लिन्ग् through a game of dice. The latter, who had a weakness for the game, succumbed; but was defeated by the wily शकुनि, uncle of the Kauravas, who played as दुर्योधन’s substitute. In the process युधिष्ठिर lost everything including his brothers, wife द्रौपदी and also himself. Then, दुर्योधन forcibly got द्रौपदी to the assembly hall and an attempt was made by दुश्शासन, the second of the Kaurava brothers, to disrobe her. Her fervent prayers to कृष्ण brought him there in an invisible form, who protected her modesty by multi-plying her robes to infinite length. Then धृतराष्ट्र, the blind king, got द्रौपदी released and restored to the Pāṇḍavas their lost wealth and kingdom. They returned to इन्द्र-prastha and resumed their rule.
However, prodded by the evil counsels of शकुनि, his uncle, दुर्योधन succeeded once again in extracting a promise from the blind king धृतराष्ट्र to challenge the Pāṇḍavas for a second round of the game of dice. युधिष्ठिर, with his proverbial weakness for the same, succumbed to it and lost his kingdom. As per the stakes he was banished to the forest. When the Pāṇḍavas were living in the forest, undergoing great hardship, कृष्ण came to know of it and arrived there to console them and advise them. कृष्ण told युधिष्ठिर that if he were at हस्तिनापुर, the capital of the Kauravas, he would have left no stone unturned to prevent the game by impressing upon all, the evils of such गम्ब्लिन्ग्.
After successfully completing the period of banishment, the Pāṇḍavas, who had gathered in Virāṭanagara, the capital of the country Matsya, celebrated the मर्रिअगे of अभिमन्यु (son of अर्जुन and सुभद्रा) with उत्तरा (daughter of the king विराट and Sudeṣṇā, his second wife). कृष्ण and बलराम attended the same. While discussing the future plans of the Pāṇḍavas in the assembly that had gathered there, कृष्ण advised them all to think of any course that will bring the good of both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas.
Seeing that दुर्योधन was obdurate in refusing to part with even the minutest part of his kingdom for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, कृष्ण decided to make a last attempt at restoring peace between them. He tried hard and sincerely, but without success.
When it was finally decided that war was the only way out for the Pāṇḍavas to get back their kingdom, कृष्ण was wooed by both the parties. When he offered the choice of the mighty Yādava army on one side or himself, but unarmed, on the other, अर्जुन chose him. दुर्योधन was happy to get the army.
Before the commencement of the war at कुरुक्षेत्र, कृष्ण tried to win over कर्ण, the king of Aṅgadeśa and a warrior of exceptional valour, to the side of the Pāṇḍavas, but, without success.
During the war which lasted for eighteen days, कृष्ण, at the request of अर्जुन, consented to be his charioteer. At the very outset, he had to deliver the great sermon, now well-known as the Bhagavadgītā, to rouse अर्जुन who, suddenly, being overcome by a moral stupor, had refused to fight.
This worked and अर्जुन fought vali-antly. कृष्ण also played many an important role, but always in defence of धर्म.
The Pāṇḍavas emerged victorious at the end and the Kauravas were decimated. After the चोरोनतिओन् of युधिष्ठिर as the king at हस्तिनापुर, कृष्ण retired to द्वारका.
After a few years, the Yādavas, the kinsmen of कृष्ण, fell into evil ways of life and exterminated one another in mutual fighting, at प्रभास, a place near द्वारका. कृष्ण taught spiritual wisdom to उद्धव, his friend and disciple, and ascended to his abode after casting off his body which was shot at by a hunter named Jara.
6. Personality of Kṛṣṇa
Whether कृष्ण-वासुदेव was a human being or God-incarnate, there is no gainsaying the fact that he has been ruling the hearts of millions of Hindus for over three millennia. If a person can make such a profound impact on the Hindu race affecting its psyche and ethos and all aspects of its life for centuries, he is no less than God. And, the Hindus do believe that he was an अवतार, God Himself come down to save mankind.
An अवतार or इन्चर्नतिओन् of God is not a product of history but creates it and shapes it. The primary purpose of an अवतार, as कृष्ण himself has stated in the Gītā (4. 7, 8) is to re-establish धर्म or righteousness on a firm foundation. This needs protecting and strengthening the hands of the good people who protect धर्म; and, if need be, subduing and eliminating the evil ones who are out to destroy it. To achieve this he will use all the powers and resources at his command. But, in the process, he does not and need not give up his human character. If at all, at times, he may transcend it, just to exhibit to the human beings the possibility of rising to superhuman levels, if only they exert themselves sufficiently.
A study of कृष्ण’s character and personality from this angle will not only be useful but also inspiring.
Throughout his life, कृष्ण’s sole concern was धर्म; to uphold it, to protect it and to reassert its supremacy; and to unravel its mystery whenever it became inscrutable.
Dharma becomes just an ethereal concept unless it lives in the minds and hearts of human beings and gets expressed through their actions. Hence, कृष्ण was very much concerned about human beings, especially the underprivileged or the weaker sections of the society as also women. The care he bestowed on the cowherds of Vṛndāvana, his curing Kubjā of her deformity, his protecting the honour of द्रौपदी at a critical moment or his bestowal of wealth on the poor कुचेल, reveal this.
Kṛṣṇa, though possessing a heart ‘softer than a flower,’ could exercise an adamantine will and terrific valour when necessary, in defence of धर्म and the dhārmic people. In fact, he was the strongest man and the greatest warrior of his times. He knew no fear, nor tasted defeat at any time in his life. The demons he killed, the tyrants he subdued were legion. He was an expert in the martial arts.
All the same, he was not a war-monger. He was a master statesman, skilled in the art of peace too. He was interested in peace; but not at the cost of धर्म.
There is a common belief that brain and brawn cannot go together. But कृष्ण was an extraordinary exception. His scholarship in the Vedic lore and the secular sciences and arts, was renowned. His three Gītās, the Bhagavadgītā, the Anugītā and the Uddhavagītā are standing monuments to his learning and wisdom.
He possessed a tremendous intellect, and an intuitive insight, coupled with immense common sense, which he often brought to bear upon knotty problems or nasty situations solving them in the best interest of all concerned. His going to हस्तिनापुर as a peace emissary, his trying to win over कर्ण to the side of the Pāṇḍavas or his apparently questionable strategies during the कुरुक्षेत्र war bespeak of this.
Intelligence and learning do not nece-ssarily lead to culture and refinement. Arrogance or craftiness is the more common result. But कृष्ण was a perfect gentleman. When he killed कṁस or got जरासन्ध eliminated, he put Ugrasena and सहदेव on the thrones though he could have easily usurped them. He was the first to honour elders, ब्राह्मणस्, sages and others, showering respect wherever it was due. Even in the face of grave provocation, he could be calm and nonchalant. The remarkable tolerance he exhibited towards the cantankerous शिशुपाल is a case to the point.
Kṛṣṇa was not only a philosopher but an accomplished योगि or mystic as well; hence the epithet ‘Yogeśvara’ applied to him (vide Gītā 18. 78). The Bhāgavata narrates several incidents wherein he had displayed yogic powers. Giving a vision of विष्णु to Akrūra, the Yādava emissary who had come to Vṛndāvana or curing Kubjā-Trivakrā of her physical handicap are instances to the point.
Mysticism and activism rarely go together; but in कृष्ण, they did. कृष्ण was ever active, ever busy, in the best interest of the world. From the cradle to the grave, his life was one continuum of dynamic activity; but always for the good of others and never for himself. The very personification of selflessness, he lived ever for others.
Kṛṣṇa as a rule, followed old customs, kept up time-honoured traditions; but would not make a fetish of the same. If in his judgment, any such custom needed to be altered or even given up, or replaced with another, he would unhesitatingly do so. He stopped the worship of god इन्द्र by the cowherds at Vṛndāvana and substituted it with the worshipping of the cows and the गोवर्धन Hill which were the backbone of their agrarian society. He acceded to अर्जुन’s request to be his charioteer, though such a job was considered to be menial, reserved for the lowborn ones because, he knew that any help rendered to the Pāṇḍavas would help the cause of धर्म.
Above all, कृष्ण was intensely human. He responded to every human emotion in an appropriate way making the persons concerned feel at home with him, even important. His parents देवकी and Vasudeva, his foster parents यशोदा and नन्द, his mates at गोकुल and Vṛndāvana, the गोपीस्, his own wives like रुक्मिणी and सत्यभामा, the Yādava chieftains, the Pāṇḍavas, the elders at हस्तिनापुर, even cows, monkeys or horses, in fact everyone that came in touch with him, was never left untouched by his magic touch of their hearts. His bewitching beauty, enchanting मुसिच् of his flute and honey-sweet words as also irrefutable लोगिच् behind them could enslave even the gods; what to speak of the poor human beings! It is but natural that he was called ‘Puruṣottama,’ the best of human beings.
7. In Defence of Kṛṣṇa
Does कृष्ण who staked his life to defend and protect the defenceless ones, himself need defence? It appears so, on the face of it, if only we look at the spate of criticisms and abuses heaped upon him by the aliens to Indian culture or decultured Indians themselves who are aliens in their own society.
At the outset, one thing has to be made clear. The criticisms levelled against कृष्ण are based on the story as depicted in the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata. These two works have declared the greatness, nay, the divinity, of कृष्ण in no uncertain terms calling him as the Supreme Lord Himself. If the detractors of कृष्ण accept as true only those parts of these works that come in handy for their criticism and conveniently ignore the rest, they are no wiser than the guy who wanted to cut an egg into two halves, keep one half for hatching chicken and use the other half for preparing an omelet!
Jesting apart, it is yet possible to offer satisfactory explanations to the objections and criticisms raised against कृष्ण.
These criticisms fall under two broad categories: those pertaining to his relationship with the गोपीस् (cowherd women) of Vṛndāvana and those related to the various stratagems he adopted to get victory for the Pāṇḍavas.
The former again, is related to two well-known incidents as given in the Bhāgavata: gopīvastrāpaharaṇa (snatching away the clothes of the गोपीस्) and रासलीला (Rāsa-dance). Neither the Viṣṇupurāṇa nor the Harivaṁśa refers to the first episode. The second is dealt with in all the three works.
Kṛṣṇa snatches away the robes of the bathing गोपीस् and perches himself atop a nearby tree along with his friends. When the गोपीस् plead for the return of their robes, he asks them to come up from water and stand with uplifted arms to receive them from him. This is the gist of the episode as given in the Bhāgavata (10.22).
The गोपीस् were kumārikās, girls in the prepuberty age-group (vide 10.22.1). कृष्ण was just seven years old (vide 10.26.3). Hence it is foolish to attribute any sexual motives to कृष्ण here. Actually, the girls were undergoing a religious vow (called कात्यायनी-vrata) to get कृष्ण as their husband! (10.22.4)
Having seen for themselves all the superhuman acts of कृष्ण even from babyhood, they were convinced of his greatness and divinity. Hence they had mentally cherished conjugal love towards him. This attitude of a सोउल् towards the Divine is well-known as kāntabhāva or मधुरभाव (bridal म्य्स्तिचिस्म्) in the works on devotion and म्य्स्तिचिस्म्. It is very much present in Christianity and Sufism too. One who wants to approach God should eschew अष्टपाशस् or eight infirmities that bind a सोउल् like ghṛṇā (hatred), śaṅkā (doubts), bhaya (fear), lajjā (shame) and so on. What is depicted here is just symbolic of this, of total surrender of the jīvas or souls to God by giving up all bonds of life; and hence should be studied in the proper perspective.
The five chapters 29 to 33, of the tenth skandha or book of the Bhāgavata, are called Rāsapañcādhyāyī and deal exclusively with कृष्ण’s play with the गोपीस्.
One moonlit night कृष्ण plays tantalizing tunes on his flute, sitting on the bank of the river यमुना. On hearing it, unable to control themselves, the गोपीस् rush to the spot.
Kṛṣṇa non-chalantly asks them the purpose of their coming to him at that hour and advises them to return home. They refuse, express their desire to enjoy his company and beg him for the same. कृष्ण obliges them with amorous sports seeing that they have totally given up everything for his sake. After some time, conceit creeps into their minds and hearts, thinking that the Lord of the universe is their mate. Sensing it, and to teach them a lesson, कृष्ण suddenly vanishes from their midst. Stricken with remorse, the गोपीस् wail and wander, pine for and pray to him. After chastising them thus, कृष्ण reappears in their midst to their great delight and dances the Rāsa-dance, multi-plying himself so that each gopī has a कृष्ण with her. All the while, the people at the homes of the गोपीस्, have not missed them at all! They continue to ‘exist’ there! This is the summary of this section.
Now, the question is: By sporting with the wives of other people, did not कृष्ण behave like an ordinary paramour? If so, was it not against even the primary norms of धर्म?
In fact, such a question was raised by the king परीक्षित् himself (vide Bhāgavata 10.33.27-29).
At the outset, an interesting fact has to be brought to light. During the राजसूय sacrifice performed by the king Yudhi-ṣṭhira, कृष्ण was chosen by the gathering for the ‘agrapūjā’ or ‘first worship’. शिशुपाल, the ruler of the Cedi kingdom, who was an inveterate enemy of कृष्ण, vehemently opposed it and rained abominable abuses upon him. But he did not so much as even mention कृष्ण’s illicit relationship with the गोपीस् of Vṛndāvana! (vide महाभारत, Sabhāparva, ch. 39 and 40) Since the Mahābhārata is the earliest of the works on कृष्ण, can we say that the gopī-episodes are the poetical fancies of the later writers who were eager to propagate the cult of Kṛṣṇabhakti or devotion to कृष्ण? Such an answer will remove the very ground from under the feet of the objectors!
However, since the Harivaṁśa, considered as an adjunct to the epic to complete the कृष्ण story, deals with the रासलीला episode, an earnest attempt can be made to meet the objection squarely. Since the objection itself is based on the भागवत, the rebuttal also should be based on the same.
The गोपीस् were not ignorant of कृष्ण’s greatness and divinity (vide Bhāgavata 10. 29. 32, 33, 37; 10.31.3, 4, 9). They had been captivated by the bewitching beauty of the कृष्ण-form, even as everyone else in the Vraja (Vṛndāvana) had been. The woman in them had got the upper hand and so, they had approached him as their lover. This type of love or approach is not unknown to human history. Many a mystic, both of the East and the West, has cultivated this type of love towards the Divine. Āṅḍāḷ, अक्क महादेवी and Mīrā of India, St. Teresa of Avila of Spain and Rabiya of Basra, Iraq are the well-known mystics who prove this point.
Kṛṣṇa was not a libertine, nor a paramour. It is the गोपीस् that approached him with love tainted by sex-passion. Considering it more as a disease that vitiates pure love, he treated them with sympathy, responding to their love, but without himself being affected by it (vide Bhāgavata 10.33.26). It is more like the parents or teachers responding to the whims of children in a healthy and dignified way, gradually leading them to wisdom. This worked and the गोपीस् were put back on the road of rectitude (ibid 10.47.18, 46; 10.82.40, 48, 49). The गोपीस् were not unchaste. They remained faithful to their husbands. The only person whom they loved, apart from their husbands, was कृष्ण and none else. This they did, knowing full well, that he was the Lord Himself.
Wonder of wonders, the men-folk of Vraja never felt that they had been separated from their wives! (ibid 10.33.38)
All this is from the subjective standpoint of कृष्ण and the गोपीस्. From the objective standpoint, did not कृष्ण transgress धर्म? If yes, has he not set a bad example to the world for centuries? This is exactly the question that the king परीक्षित् put to the sage शुक, the narrator of the Bhāgavata (vide 10.33. 27-29).
Śuka in his reply classifies men into three groups: the Īśvaras (Lords, Incarnations), the jīvanmuktas (the liberated ones) and the ordinary people.
Those who realize God in this very life are called jīvanmuktas. According to the Hindu scriptures like the उपनिषद्स्, they have transcended even धर्म and hence are not bound by the dos and don’ts of this world. Nor are they tainted even by grave sins (vide Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1).
These jīvanmuktas get that power by meditating on the lotus feet of God. Then, what to speak of कृष्ण, who is God Himself! He can transgress the ordinary norms of धर्म for extraordinary ends in life, which are always for the good of others. The acts of such Īśvaras cannot be and should not be emulated by the ordinary beings. शिव drank the deadly poison हालाहल. Fire can destroy everything it touches. But ordinary mortals can never do it. कृष्ण responded to the love of the गोपीस् for their sake and never for his own sake. Even in doing so he multiplied himself, out of his māyā power, to be with them all simultaneously. He was also, at the same time, present as गोपीस् in their houses, doing their normal work. Hence, the supra-dhārmic doings of Īśvaras like कृष्ण cannot be and should not be emulated by the ordinary run of mankind. If someone can do all that कृष्ण did, then, he, like कृष्ण, is an ईश्वर and so, can take liberties with धर्म!
That is why Swami Vivekānanda, whose life was unsullied and whose criticism spared none who was not above board, has spoken of कृष्ण at Vṛndāvana in these glorious terms: ‘Ah! that most marvellous passage of his life, the most difficult to understand, and which none ought to attempt to understand until he has become perfectly chaste and pure, that most marvellous expansion of love, allegorized and expressed in that beautiful play at Vrindaban, which none can under-stand but he who has become mad with love, drunk deep of the cup of love! Who can understand the throes of the love of the Gopis—the very ideal of love, love that wants nothing, love that even does not care for हेअवेन्, love that does not care for anything in this world or the world to come?... A great landmark in the history of religion is here, the ideal of love for love’s sake, duty for duty’s sake, and it for the first time fell from the lips of the greatest of Incarnations, Krishna, and for the first time, in the history of humans, upon the soil of India.’ (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, Vol. 3, 1984 edn., pp. 257-258.)
Allied to this is the criticism that कृष्ण had married 16,008 wives, a staggering number by any standards! The ‘aṣṭamahiṣīs’ were the eight queens, chief among them being रुक्मिणी and सत्य-bhāmā. The other 16,000 were the princesses he had saved from the prison of the demon नरक. Since they had been practically deserted by their relatives, कृष्ण gave them shelter for which ceremonial मर्रिअगे was a necessity. And, पोल्य्गम्य् was quite common among kings and princes during those days. It is important to note that the divine sage नारद, once, out of curiosity, visited the houses of all the wives of कृष्ण and found him there (Bhāgavata 10.69).
Sometimes an esoteric interpretation is given to this. The number 16,000 really represents 16, the zeros being the reflection of poetic fancies. And, this 16 actually represents the 16 parts of the human personality with which the jīvātman, the individual सोउल्, is associated. They are: five organs of perception, five organs of action, five vital airs and the मिन्द्. The jīvātman is the lord of all these 16 parts. Hence they are allegorically represented as his wives. Since, in the ultimate analysis (as per Advaita Vedānta) the jīvātman is identical with परमात्मन् or God, कृष्ण is depicted as having 16(000) wives.
An allegorical interpretation is also given for the love of the गोपीस् towards कृष्ण. The गोपीस् represent the jīvas or the individual souls pining for reunion with the परमात्मन् or the Supreme सोउल् who is कृष्ण, from whom they have been separated.
The second category of objections that pertain to कृष्ण’s way of handling the various problems that arose during the कुरुक्षेत्र war may now be taken up. He is accused of political perfidy and Machiavellian methods in his dealings with the Kauravas. It is therefore necessary to examine the various episodes and incidents of the Mahābhārata and get at the truth. They may be listed and tackled as follows:
1. He tried to break the friendship of कर्ण with दुर्योधन and wean him away from the Kauravas.
Kṛṣṇa never wanted the fratricidal war of कुरुक्षेत्र to take place. Having failed in his peace mission due to the recalcitrance of दुर्योधन, he made a final attempt to somehow stop it by revealing to कर्ण the well-kept secret that he was really the first son born to कुन्ती. If कर्ण had agreed to defect to the Pāṇḍava side, दुर्योधन, having come to know the truth, might have agreed to his being the king of half the kingdom and both the groups could have lived in peace. कर्ण was the best friend and the main source of strength of दुर्योधन. His loss would certainly have had a demoralizing effect on दुर्योधन forcing him for a compromise. Thus bloodshed would have been avoided and धर्म kept up. Hence what कृष्ण did was really a master stroke of statesmanship.
2. Though he had taken the vow of renouncing weapons and not fight during the war, he broke the same and attacked भीष्म.
When भीष्म was fighting so fiercely that the Pāṇḍava forces were being merci-lessly destroyed or put on the run, कृष्ण found that अर्जुन was not putting forth his best against भीष्म due to an inherent softness towards him. It was then that कृष्ण decided to take up his discus and attack भीष्म himself. He was stopped by अर्जुन halfway with the promise of doing his best (Mahābhārata, Bhīṣmaparva, 59.103). Then, कृष्ण returned to the chariot.
The act of कृष्ण was more to induce and inspire अर्जुन than himself fight भीष्म. Again, the primary purpose of कृष्ण’s life was to uphold and protect धर्म. For him no sacrifice was too great compared to this task; and, transgressing a vow when needed was a part of the same.
It is necessary to mention here that the popular story that भीष्म too had vowed that he would force कृष्ण to take to arms and that कृष्ण, pleased by his intense devotion, obliged him by breaking his own vow is not found in the Mahābhārata.
3. कृष्ण induced युधिष्ठिर to tell a lie (‘aśvatthāmā hataḥ’—Aśvatthāmā has been killed) camouflaging it like truth, by adding the words ‘kuñjaraḥ’ (‘elephant’), to force the invincible Droṇa to retire from the battle.
The original verse in the Mahābhārata attributed to युधिष्ठिर is: tamatathyabhaye magno jaye sakto yudhiṣṭhiraḥ । aśvatthāmā hata iti śabdamuccaiścacāra ha । avyaktamabravīd rājan hataḥ kuñjara ityuta ॥ (Droṇaparva 190.55). ‘Yudhiṣṭhira, O king, afraid of telling an untruth, but interested in victory, addressed Droṇa thus in a loud voice: “Aśvatthāmā is dead.” But, he also added the words, “The elephant is dead” in an inaudible voice’.
If we accept this version as a part of the original text (and not an inter-polation), then we will be obliged to concede that युधिष्ठिर told a blatant lie at the instance of कृष्ण, to discomfit Droṇa, notwithstanding the fact that भीम had just then killed an elephant of the same name, Aśvatthāmā.
But, fortunately, there are strong reasons to believe that this is an interpolation carelessly added by a raw hand at a later period. The same may now be summarized briefly as follows:
a. Contrary to the common belief, Droṇa did not lay down arms, even on hearing this shocking news, but continued to fight, routing धृष्टद्युम्न and others. Thus, the very purpose of telling that lie has been nullified (Droṇaparva, ch. 191).
b. It is unthinkable that भीम, fearlessness personified, who dared to face even the Nārāyaṇāstra discharged by Aśvatthāmā against the advice and persuasion of even कृष्ण, would stoop to such mean levels as killing an elephant by name ‘Aśvatthāmā’ and give grist to the mill of falsehood. It is, by the same standards, absurd to think that Yudhi-ṣṭhira, the धर्मराज (king of धर्म), would have allowed himself to utter a falsehood, that too against his preceptor; and that, कृष्ण, the very purpose of whose life was to establish धर्म, could be the originator of such a heinous plan.
c. Since Droṇa was killing innocent warriors on the battlefield by using formidable weapons like the ब्रह्मास्त्र, against the norms prescribed for the discharge of such missiles, several sages like विश्वामित्र, जमदग्नि, भरद्वाज, गौतम, अत्रि, वसिष्ठ, भृगु and others, arrived there and remonstrated with him, urging him to renounce his weapons and return to the spiritual path which he had given up out of delusion (ibid 190. 32-40). They also reminded him that his time was up and death was imminent.
It was this that ultimately made Droṇa retire from the battle and sit in meditation at which time, धृष्टद्युम्न (son of king Drupada) beheaded him.
We can safely conclude from this that this part of the story that maligns Yudhi-ṣṭhira and कृष्ण is a clumsy interpolation which serves no purpose. 4
It will not be out of place here to mention another incident from the Mahā-bhārata (Karṇaparva, chs. 68-71) which brings out brilliantly कृष्ण’s character and wisdom. अर्जुन, in a moment of impulse, had taken a vow that he would decapitate anyone that would speak disparagingly of his celebrated bow, गाण्डीव. Once, on the battlefield, युधिष्ठिर was routed by कर्ण and barely managed to escape with his life. When अर्जुन came to enquire about his welfare, learning that कर्ण had not yet been killed by अर्जुन, युधिष्ठिर abused him and taunted him to part with his गाण्डीव. ‘True’ to his vow, अर्जुन was about to attack युधिष्ठिर, when कृष्ण intervened. After learning of his vow, कृष्ण brought wisdom to his मिन्द् through a wonderful discourse on धर्म (righteousness) and सत्य (truth).
This is the gist of his discourse: सत्य is that which is sanctioned by धर्म and असत्य (untruth) is that which is not. धर्म is that which brings about lokahita or good to the world. Hence, the test of सत्य is whether it will result in good to the world. Looked at from this angle, an असत्य which brings about good to the world is सत्य; and a सत्य which harms the world is असत्य!
4. कृष्ण tricked Jayadratha by creating artificial darkness, hiding the orb of the sun through his disc सुदर्शन, and got him killed by अर्जुन.
Jayadratha, the king of सिन्धु country was the brother-in-law of the Kauravas and was fighting on their side. Once he had abducted द्रौपदी, when the Pāṇḍavas were living in the forest. He was however caught and punished, and द्रौपदी was rescued from his clutches. Later, he was primarily responsible in preventing the four Pāṇḍavas (without अर्जुन) from coming to the rescue of the young अभिमन्यु (son of सुभद्रा and अर्जुन) who had been trapped inside the Cakravyūha or wheel formation of the Kaurava army. This had resulted in the cruel murder of the boy by the so-called warriors and against all norms of the battle. On coming to know of it, अर्जुन had vowed that he would kill Jayadratha before sunset, the next day or immolate himself by entering fire. The Kauravas were frightened by this terrible vow and tried their best to hide Jayadratha from अर्जुन’s view. Though अर्जुन fought fiercely and relentlessly till the evening there was no sign of the targeted enemy. At that time कृष्ण, by his योग power (and not by सुदर्शन discus) created subjective darkness in Jayadratha, who out of joy and relief stuck his head out, but was killed by अर्जुन (Droṇaparva ch. 146. 64-68). Since Jayadratha was fighting on the side of अधर्म or unrighteousness and had sinned on two counts, it is but proper that अर्जुन killed him and that कृष्ण who was working for the re-establishment of धर्म, aided him.
5. कृष्ण incited अर्जुन to kill कर्ण eventhough the latter was unarmed and was trying to lift up his chariot which had run aground. This was a cowardly act, against all norms of धर्म.
The fact is that कर्ण was not killed when in a disarmed or helpless condition. He died fighting in the usual way.
This incident is narrated in detail in the Karṇaparva (chs. 90, 91). The rebuttal given by कृष्ण to कर्ण (ch. 90. 1-14) was so logical and powerful that कर्ण had to swallow it in shame (vide 90. 15).
Kṛṣṇa’s argument was simple. When the Kauravas had flouted all norms of धर्म in trying to kill or harm the Pāṇḍavas—reflected in their trying to poison भीम, destroy them all through arson, molest their wife द्रौपदी and snatch away their kingdom through the deceitful game of dice—and since कर्ण had abetted in their crimes, he had forfeited all claims to धर्म!
6. During the गदा-युद्ध (mace-fight) between भीम and दुर्योधन, कृष्ण reminded भीम of his vow to break दुर्योधन’s thighs by slapping his own thigh, though hitting below the navel was prohibited in such fights.
Actually it was अर्जुन who did it after hearing कृष्ण’s comments on the fight, since दुर्योधन was slowly getting the upper hand (vide Śalyaparva ch. 58.21).
Though it was against the rules of the mace fight, भीम had to do it since he had vowed to break दुर्योधन’s left thigh at the time when the latter had indecently showed to द्रौपदी his bared lap (vide Sabhāparva ch. 69.10-14). If this had not been done, कृष्ण averred, then, दुर्योधन would have won and would have continued to rule the kingdom persisting in his evil ways, bringing misery upon all. When the choice was between losing धर्म on earth or breaking a rule in the duel, the lesser evil was chosen. It is like amputating a limb to save life.
7. कृष्ण did not prevent the fratricidal fight among the Yādavas though he was capable of doing so. On the other hand he too joined in it.
The Yādavas as a race, had degene-rated beyond redemption due to severe addiction to drinking. All efforts of कृष्ण to reform them had proved futile. Since कृष्ण was for dharma and never for his own people, his role in the destruction of the Yādavas who had given up धर्म is rather laudable!
8. कृष्ण’s end was ignominious since he was assassinated by an ordinary hunter.
Kṛṣṇa left his body out of his own free will, in योग (Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.37.75). According to the Bhāgavata (11.31.6) he ascended to his world with the body (since it was divine).
The story of Jara, the hunter, killing कृष्ण may be an allegorical way of describing that कृष्ण left the body in old age (jarā = old age).
Even if the story is taken to be literally true, there is nothing in it that lowers कृष्ण’s prestige. The manner of discarding the physical body, after the purpose of life has been achieved, is left to the person concerned and does not affect his greatness in any way. बुद्ध was poisoned. Jesus was crucified like ordinary criminals. Some of the Sikh Gurus died as martyrs at the hands of barbarians.
Not only the manner of death, even insults heaped upon such great ones while they were living, neither affected them nor their reputation. For instance, महावीर was spat upon. Sri Ramakrishna was kicked by a greedy treacherous priest. Since they practised ahimsā as the highest धर्म, they never retaliated. On the other hand, they blessed these sinners. But, today, the world continues to adore them. In fact, these very incidents have made them shine even more brilliantly.
8. Teachings of Kṛṣṇa
Kṛṣṇa was as great a master in the spiritual sciences as he was in the secular ones. His immortal teachings have been left to us through three great works: Bhagavadgītā, Anugītā and Uddhavagītā. The first two are a part of the well-known epic, Mahābhārata and the last, of Bhāgavata.
BHAGAVADGĪTĀ
The Bhagavadgītā is the most celebrated of these and has been con-sidered as a monumental work in the religio-philosophical literature of India for centuries. It is a part of the Bhīṣmaparva (Ch. 25 to 42). It is in the form of a dialogue between कृष्ण and अर्जुन spread over 18 chapters, comprising 700 verses.
Just at the commencement of the कुरुक्षेत्र war, after his chariot has been stationed in between the armies of the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, but right in front of the venerable भीष्म and the preceptor Droṇa, अर्जुन sees them as also the others arrayed against him and collapses due to mental depression. He refuses to fight after narrating his reasons to do so. His arguments boil down to this: Killing is a sin. Killing one’s own kith and kin, that too for the sake of a paltry kingdom, is worse. It is far better to renounce the world and take to begging to maintain oneself.
Kṛṣṇa’s reply to this is direct and clear. Here, the basic question is not whether to fight and kill or to retire from it. The basic question is whether to punish those who, impelled by greed and selfishness, have transgressed all norms of धर्म with impunity; or to let them enjoy the fruits of their heinous crimes. This war has been foisted upon the Pāṇḍavas by the irascible दुर्योधन even though they have tried all means at their command to avoid it. Since the society expects the क्षत्त्रिय prince to protect its life, possessions and values, which duty it has put on his shoulders, अर्जुन (and the Pāṇḍavas) have no other go but to fight in defence of these.
As to the question of killing or dying, कृष्ण states that the essential nature of all beings is आत्मन्, the Self. It has no birth, no change, no disease nor death. It is the body worn by the सोउल् like an apparel, that is born or that dies. Hence, there need be no misgivings about the sin of killing or the fear of dying. Even supposing that our birth and death are coterminous with those of the body, there is no cause for sorrow since this is inevitable in life.
Kṛṣṇa avers that no living being can avoid activity or work. Hence one must learn to perform one’s duties and discharge one’s responsibilities,—Kṛṣṇa calls this as ‘svadharma’—however unpleasant they may appear to be. The reaction of work on the मिन्द्, whether it is pleasant or unpleasant, is due to the emotional attachment one has towards it and its results. If one can learn to do one’s work as best as one can, without attachment or aversion, as a matter of duty or to serve the world or to please God, then, it brings about internal peace and equani-mity. This mode of working is known as ‘niṣkāmakarmayoga’.
Incidentally and in reply to अर्जुन’s several questions, कृष्ण deals with many other topics too. He accepts the यज्ञ-system, the system of sacrifices in duly consecrated Vedic fires, but expands the scope of the word ‘yajña’ by calling any act of self-sacrifice and public good as a यज्ञ, no less than its Vedic counterpart. Thus, donating one’s wealth to the needy can be called ‘dravyayajña’ (dravya = wealth or money); imparting knowledge to others becomes ‘jñānayajña’ and so on.
Kṛṣṇa has christened as ‘śreṣṭha’ anyone who works for the good of the world and advises him to be extremely careful in his personal and public life so as to set a model to others.
Kṛṣṇa also deals with the several paths to perfection like ज्ञानयोग (the योग of knowledge), भक्तियोग (the योग of devotion to God) and ध्यानयोग (the योग of meditation) and equates कर्मयोग (the योग of selfless action) with them.
Another teaching of tremendous hope given by कृष्ण is the assurance that he, the Lord, will come down as an ‘avatāra’ or incarnate himself here, whenever धर्म declines and अधर्म gains in momentum. There are no conditions with regard to time and place in this act of grace. And, this doctrine of अवतार has been enunciated for the very first time in the Hindu scriptures, in the Bhagavadgītā (4.6-8).
Kṛṣṇa reveals his divinity by vouchsafing to अर्जुन his Cosmic Form (viśvarūpa) so as to strengthen his faith. Towards the end कृष्ण advises अर्जुन to surrender himself to Him with the assurance of freeing him from all sins.
Arjuna shakes off his delusion and rouses himself to action to defend धर्म.
ANUGĪTĀ
The Anugītā, the second of the three Gītās attributed to कृष्ण, is also a part of the epic Mahābhārata (Aśvamedhaparva, chs. 16 to 51). It comprises 1056 verses spread over 36 chapters.
Having completed his task of restoring their kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas so that they can rule according to धर्म, कृष्ण has decided to return to द्वारका. Wishing to take advantage of his spiritual wisdom before his departure, अर्जुन requests him to teach him once again the great spiritual knowledge which he had taught at the start of the कुरुक्षेत्र war. Chiding अर्जुन for having forgotten such a profound teaching and pleading his inability to bring back to memory all that teaching once again, कृष्ण proceeds to teach him through ‘itihāsa’ or ancient stories.
Avoiding these rather involved stories, the gist of the teachings may be given here. The first topic dealt with is that of the जीव, the individual सोउल्, how he gets out of the body and how he gets into another, after death. Both these depend upon the कर्म (action) he has done. Good कर्म takes him to स्वर्ग or हेअवेन्, bad कर्म to नरक or हेल्ल्. He then returns to this human birth to continue his journey. If he takes to the path of धर्म, he is gradually led towards मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
The next topic is how a human being can attain मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. Anyone who has cultivated virtues like equanimity, intense desire for मोक्ष, renunciation and self-control, becomes fit for मोक्ष. By adopting the path of योग in which self-control, austerity, contemplation on the आत्मन् or the Self within, desirelessness and peace are important sādhanas, he will be able to attain the Abode of ब्रह्मन्.
The third topic, expounded in the form of a dialogue between a ब्राह्मण and his wife—hence called Brāhmaṇagītā—comprises miscellaneous subjects like the आत्मन्-ब्रह्मन् principle which is beyond the ken of the senses, meditating on the functioning of the senses and the मिन्द् as a यज्ञ or sacrifice, importance of the पञ्चप्राणस् or the five vital airs, the greatness of जनक, the king of मिथिला who had conquered mamakāra or the sense of possessions and the state of a jīvanmukta, one liberated even while living in the body.
Then, अर्जुन questions कृष्ण about the path that leads to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. कृष्ण in his reply states that the परमात्मन्, or the Supreme Self, residing in the hearts of all, is to be realized through तपस् or austerity, for which सṁन्यास (life of renunciation) is the best means. Trying to see one Self in all and giving up all that obstructs this, is a part of this discipline.
This is followed by a description of the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and tamas—and their products like अहङ्कार (egoity) and the five elements like earth and water.
Then comes a description of the four āśramas or stages of life (brahmacarya, गार्हस्थ्य, वानप्रस्थ and सṁन्यास), the allegory of the ‘Brahmavṛkṣa’ (actually the human body, compared to a tree) and how it can be cut by the sword of ज्ञान (spiritual wisdom), some discussions about धर्म or religious duties and activities, and the efficacy of तपस् or austerity in the form of self-control, which can destroy sins and give spiritual enlightenment. The Anugītā ends with this.
UDDHAVAGĪTĀ
Unlike these two Gītās, the Uddhava-gītā is not a part of the epic Mahābhārata, but of the Bhāgavata. It comprises 23 chapters (chs. 7 to 29 of the eleventh skandha or book) and has 1030 verses.
Having intuited the imminent destruction of his race of the Yadus by mutual fighting, कृष्ण decides to return to his divine Abode. Realizing this, उद्धव, an intimate companion and devotee, approaches him for guidance. कृष्ण then teaches him spiritual wisdom and directs him to go to the बदरिकाश्रम in the हिमालयस्.
Kṛṣṇa commences his teaching with an ancient story. king यदु, the son of ययाति, once saw an अवधूत, a perfect being (who had shaken off all bonds born out of इग्नोरन्चे), and asked him how he had attained to that state of freedom and bliss. The अवधूत replied that he had learnt his lessons from 24 teachers: patience from earth; non-attachment from wind which is not tainted by the smell it carries; purification from water; power to destroy evil, from fire; living for the good of others from the sun; indifference towards the world from a python; dangers of temptation from a moth; the desirability of collecting good teachings from all available sources, from a bee; the need to conquer the instinct of sex and taste from an elephant and a fish; the need to conquer desires, from a courtesan; the necessity of living alone, to progress in the inner life from a girl and so on.
Then कृष्ण proceeds to tell उद्धव that कर्म or action binds a person to transmigratory existence. Hence one should renounce evil actions and actions motivated by desires; but perform ordained or obligatory duties without the desire for fruits. He clarifies that सṁसार or transmigratory existence is due to attachment to the body and, the आत्मन् or Self is never subject to it.
He then describes the characteristics of the bound and the free souls. Bondage comes from egoism and attachment to the body. Freedom results from detachment.
At the specific request of उद्धव, कृष्ण delineates the signs of साधुस् or holy beings and of devotion to God. Compassion, truthfulness, self-control, devotion to duties, equanimity under all conditions, fortitude—these are some of the traits found in साधुस्. Devotion to God (or कृष्ण) manifests itself as worship of images, interest in listening to the stories of the Lord, cultivation of certain attitudes of love, going on पिल्ग्रिमगे, observing religious festivities and so on. A true devotee is deeply interested in serving the Lord through rituals, and is devoid of pride and self-praise. Satsaṅga or cultivating the company of devotees and holy beings is the best means of attaining God.
Continuing, कृष्ण describes the three guṇas or qualities of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस् and stresses the need to overcome the last two but augment the first. This leads to devotion and knowledge.
Then comes a description of ध्यान or meditation on God. The mode of sitting, method of प्राणायाम or breath-control and contemplation on the beautiful form of कृष्ण-विष्णु are dealt with in detail. The अष्टसिद्धिस् or the eight psychic powers that result by yogic practices are also touched upon; but the योगि is advised against taking interest in them since they are obstacles to spiritual enlightenment.
Uddhava now puts a question: ‘O Lord! What are the various ways in which the sages contemplate you and attain the सिद्धिस् or powers?’ कृष्ण in reply, states how he is the best in all things, their very essence. For instance, he is the Self, friend and inner controller of all beings. He is विष्णु among the Ādityas and Nīlalohita among the Rudras. He is भृगु among the great sages, प्रह्लाद among the दैत्यस् or demons, वासुकि and अनन्त among the serpents, lion among the animals, गङ्गा among the rivers, हिमालयस् among the mountains, उद्धव among the devotees and so on. In fact, wherever there is excellence, he is that. 5
Uddhava is now interested to know those dharmas or duties that are conducive to the development of devotion. In reply कृष्ण gives a fairly detailed account of the well-known varṇāśrama-dharmas, duties of the four castes and stages of life.
Kṛṣṇa then proceeds to declare that all duality that appears here, is only māyā, इल्लुसिओन् and hence unreal. He, the basis of all, alone is Real. उद्धव then requests कृष्ण to teach him ज्ञान and भक्ति by which one can attain मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. In reply कृष्ण expounds them. ज्ञान or knowledge is that by which one knows that परमात्मन्, the Supreme Self, is in everything; He is everything. Since karmas or ritualistic actions give transient fruits, one should not get attached to them. भक्ति or devotion arises as a result of listening to and reciting the stories of the Lord, of worshipping the Lord and honouring His devotees. Renunci-ation of worldly desires and worldly objects of pleasure strengthens भक्ति.
Kṛṣṇa, at the request of उद्धव, further expounds the various spiritual disciplines that are conducive to ज्ञान and भक्ति. They are: यम and नियम comprising the disciplines like अहिṁसा (non-injury), सत्य (truth), जप (repetition of the divine name), तपस् (austerities), पूजा (worship), paropakāra (helping the needy), ācāryasevā (serving the preceptor) and so on; शम (concentrating the मिन्द् on the Lord); दम (self control); तितिक्षा (forbearance); dhṛti (controlling the instincts of taste and sex); सṁन्यास (renunciation of the fruits of action) and so on. 6
Continuing further, कृष्ण describes the three well-known yogas: ज्ञानयोग, कर्मयोग and भक्तियोग. An intense spirit of renunciation is a must for the first. Renouncing evil actions and the fruits of the good ones is a precondition for the second. Interest and faith in listening to the stories of the Lord is a quality needed for the third.
This is then followed by a discussion about the various philosophical truths and principles given in other works like प्रकृति (nature) and पुरुष (soul). The mode of rebirth of an ignorant being, due to that very इग्नोरन्चे, is also stated.
Uddhava now raises a pertinent question: How should a devotee react to the evil behaviour of evil persons? कृष्ण, in reply, narrates the story of a भिक्षु (mendicant) who put up bravely with the harassment of unsympathetic and evil persons. (This section is known as the Bhikṣugītā.) There was a rich man in the country of Avantī. He was a miser and treated even his own wife, children and other relatives with scant regard. The gods were offended with him. So, he lost everything, being cheated by his own people. His troubles gave rise to wisdom and a genuine spirit of renunciation. He then became an itinerant mendicant. Whenever he moved out, begging for alms, evil people who had known his earlier life, started harassing him in many ways including violent physical assaults. However, accepting everything as the fruit of his evil karmas, he never retaliated nor reacted in any way, practising extreme forbearance, without any rancour in his heart. He then sang unto his own मिन्द्, a poem containing nuggets of great spiritual wisdom. The gist of that poem—the Bhikṣugītā—is that it is one’s own मिन्द् that is responsible for weal or woe, and that one who conquers his own मिन्द् is the Master of even gods! And, this can be achieved by devotion to God.
Some discussions about getting rid of मोह or delusion by Sāṅkhyayoga or the path of knowledge, as also a description of the three guṇas and their products follow next.
The obstacles created by lust in the path of योग are described by narrating the story of पुरूरवस्. The need for and the tremendous advantages of cultivating satsaṅga or company of the holy ones is the topic that comes next.
This is followed by a rather detailed description of पूजा or ritualistic worship of God. A brief summary of the items involved in the worship can be given as follows: bath and wearing clean clothes suitable for पूजा; keeping the image or symbol of worship; preliminary processes of ritual purification (called न्यास); आवाहन or inviting the Lord into the image or symbol; offering sandal paste, flowers, incense, lamp and items of ड़ोओद्. On special occasions होम (offering oblations into a duly consecrated fire) may also be done. The whole worship can be concluded with recitation of hymns and salutation. Faith and devotion are most important in such worship.
After stressing once again that the external world is only an appearance, that the आत्मन् or Self is the spirit beyond the body-मिन्द् complex and giving some methods of योग that help in overcoming the obstacles to the inner life, कृष्ण concludes his teaching with a description of a paṇḍita, a man of spiritual wisdom who has attained equanimity. उद्धव then departs for the बदरिकाश्रम in the हिमालयस् with a heavy heart, due to the pain of separation from कृष्ण.
9. Kṛṣṇa’s Philosophy of Life
He lives long that lives well! He alone lives, who lives for others! And, कृष्ण did all these: He lived long; he lived for others and so, he lived well!
The philosophy of life that कृष्ण has taught us can best be learnt from his own life. The basic note of the मुसिच् of his life was धर्म. And, to him, anything that brought about the good of the individual and the society, the two being in consonance with each other, was धर्म. Whenever there was a conflict between these two, it was the social good that he preferred.
There are three recognized sources of धर्म: the śāstras or the Holy Books; the सम्प्रदाय or tradition set up by a long line of ṛṣis or sages; and, one’s own purified मिन्द्. कृष्ण followed them all in his personal life. He performed all the rituals prescribed for his station in life, did his duties, honoured the elders, the ब्राह्मणस् and the sages and took good care of all his dependents.
Dharma is protected and nourished when institutions and the people running the institutions follow धर्म unhindered. कृष्ण was ever ready to protect them both. If, in the process, confrontation with the wicked was necessary, he was the first to rise against them in defence of धर्म.
The Bhāgavata (1.3.28) has called him as भगवान्, the Lord Himself (kṛṣṇastu भगवान् svayam). He is the पुरुषोत्तम, the best of men, of the Bhagavadgītā (15.18). Hence, there was no need for him to be engaged in action, either to get or get rid of anything in life. And yet, he worked relentlessly; but, only for the sake of others, for the good of the world. He never had any axe to grind. He was unselfish to the core.
Furthermore, his work, his actions, were always perfect. He was as skilled in the art of love and compassion as in war; as dexterous in speaking honey and milk to the suffering ones, as in chiding or deriding hotheaded renegades. He was easily controlled by pure love, but adam-antine to those that hated him and fought with him. He was ever forgiving to the meek and the humble, but an inveterate enemy of the cheats and the hypocrites.
Fearlessness personified, he was ever ready to face any problem in life. But he always tried his best to defuse nasty situations before they grew into knotty problems.
Above all, he was completely detached, the very picture of supreme unconcern.
Finally, he was Yogeśvara, the master of योग and Yogīśvara, the master of yogis too. He never forgot to teach the highest spiritual verities to those that sought them.
This, then, is what he has taught us to emulate: Be ever active for the sake of धर्म, for the good of others; but never be selfish. Do your work as best as you can. Follow धर्म and have firm faith that it will protect you. Do not run away from the problems of life; but face them boldly. Pray to God and He will give you the strength needed to face them or transcend them. Never forget that the final goal of life is लिबेरतिओन्. Strive your best to attain it through ज्ञान and भक्ति, and be free!
10. Rādhā
In the popular religious lore of the Hindus राधा has been very intimately associated with कृष्ण. Hence it is but meet that a few lines be devoted to her here.
At the outset, it must be mentioned that राधा is nowhere to be seen in the four well-known sources of the कृष्ण story: Mahābhārata, Harivaṁśa, Viṣṇupurāṇa and Bhāgavata. There is a reference in the Bhāgavata (10.30.25 ff.) to a fortunate gopī who had gone alone with कृष्ण just before the Rāsakrīḍā. The words used here—anayārādhitaḥ (= being propitiated by her)—might have provided the seeds for the later concept of राधा, as the gopī dearest to कृष्ण.
The story of राधा in detail appears in the Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa of the Brahma-vaivartapurāṇa, a late work. She is described here as having emerged out of कृष्ण and as his शक्ति or power. It is, perhaps, the poet जयदेव (A. D. 1200) that has immortalized her through his well-known lyric, Gītagovinda. Bengal वैष्णविस्म् nourished by चैतन्य (A. D. 1485-1533) and others, has given her a unique place in its कृष्ण theology and metaphysics.
It is plausible that the ‘Prakṛti-प्रधान’ (Mother Nature) of the earlier Sāṅkhya system of philosophy has gradually got metamorphosed into the राधा personality of the later Vaiṣṇava schools of theology.
11. Kṛṣṇa Festivals
Generally, every religion has three aspects: philosophy, म्य्थोलोग्य् and rituals. Philosophy tries to deal with the ultimate truths and values. म्य्थोलोग्य् tries to present them to the masses in a language that they can understand. Rituals, by affording opportunities to practise religion, fulfil an emotional need.
Festivals in हिन्दुइस्म् are legion. A few of the more important ones, directly related to the कृष्ण legends, will be outlined here.
The most important of these is Kṛṣṇa-janmāṣṭamī, the birthday of कृष्ण. He was born on the aṣṭamī or the eighth day of the kṛṣṇapakṣa or dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa (August-September) at midnight. The नक्षत्र or constellation was रोहिणी. Generally this comes the next day. Hence that day is called Jayantī. Both the days are important though the actual worship has to be done at midnight on the aṣṭamī day.
Fasting for the whole day and night, worship of कृष्ण in image or picture, keeping vigil throughout the night, listening to the stories and exploits of कृष्ण, recitation of the Bhāgavata, singing of hymns and songs, and जप (repetition of the divine name) of the famous मन्त्र Om namo bhagavate Vāsudevāya are the essential parts of this festival.
In मथुरा and Vṛndāvan, the two towns associated with कृष्ण’s birth and childhood, there are a number of temples dedicated to him. जन्माष्टमी is celebrated there on a grand scale.
It may be of interest to state here that in Maharashtra, it is the practice, particularly of boys and the common folk, to hang up pots full of curds and buttermilk on the day after the birth of कृष्ण is celebrated, to play underneath the pots and get drenched by the curds and buttermilk running out from the holes made by the boys, in typical कृष्ण fashion!
The birthday of राधा or Rādhikā, the gopī dearest to कृष्ण, is celebrated as Rādhāṣṭamī, on Bhādrapada śukla aṣṭamī (eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, September). During this festival, worship is offered to राधा and कृष्ण together. One should subsist on fruits only on this day. Apart from hearing and singing devotional मुसिच्, one should also listen to certain episodes from the Brahmavaivartapurāṇa related to राधा and कृष्ण.
Govardhanapūjā (worship of the hill गोवर्धन of मथुरा) which includes Annakūṭa (‘mountain or heap of ड़ोओद्’) is another festival, more commonly observed in North India, related to कृष्ण. It is observed on the first day of the bright half of the month of Kārttika (Kārttika śukla pratipad—generally in November), a day after the famous दीपावली (Diwali) festival. Worship of the गोवर्धन hill and कृष्ण as Gopāla (cowherd boy), decorating and worshipping the cows, calves and bulls, keeping vigil in the night as also contemplating on the कृष्ण story are its salient features. Of course, the गोवर्धन hill can be worshipped only in मथुरा (Uttar Pradesh). Elsewhere, a replica is made, generally in cowdung, for purposes of worship. A big heap of ड़ोओद्, comprising various items of eatables, should also be prepared resembling a hill, and worshipped. This is the Annakūṭa festival.
When the festival of revelry, the होलि or Holikā, is celebrated all over the country, Bengal celebrates it as Dolāyātrā or Dolotsava (festival of the swing). It is observed for three or five days from the 14th day of the dark half of the month Phālguna (March) (phālguna कृष्ण caturdaśī ). Worship of अग्नि or the fire-god, worship of कृष्ण in an image stationed in a dolā or swing and swinging it for 7 times on the first day and 21 times on the last day are the chief elements of this festival.
The day on which कृष्ण taught the Bhagavadgītā to अर्जुन, called Gītā-jayantī, falls on the eleventh day of the bright half of the month Mārgaśira (December) (Mārgaśira śukla एकादशी). It is celebrated with ड़स्तिन्ग्, worship of कृष्ण as Gītācārya (preceptor of the Gītā), chanting of the Gītā and listening to discourses on the same.
12. Conclusion
For aeons if कृष्ण has been an agonizing enigma to some, he has put millions into ecstasies. There is nothing to wonder at in this. His very name ‘Kṛṣṇa-वासुदेव’ solves this riddle. Etymolgoically speaking, ‘Kṛṣṇa’ is one who is ever blissful and ever attracts others to himself (vide Viṣṇusahasranāma 57). ‘Vāsudeva’ is the Divinity that pervades everything in the universe and is also immanent in it (ibid 332).
So, कृष्ण as a human being, extremely handsome and intensely affectionate, has been driving the votaries into rapturous moods. But as God or God’s इन्चर्नतिओन् on earth, his ways have been inscrutable.
The word ‘Kṛṣṇa’ also means ‘dark’, ‘mysterious’. He was dark in colour and his ways were mysterious!
The ocean appears to be dark from a distance. But when we approach it and take its water into our hands, the water is pure and colourless. Similarly, कृष्ण is a problem and a riddle only from a distance. When approached with love and faith, the dark mist of misunderstanding dissolves into a crystal clear experience of divine bliss and eternal presence.
Kṛṣṇa is true to his word: ‘In whichever way people approach me, in the same way do I respond.’ (Gītā 4.11.) If we approach him as ‘problem-कृष्ण’ he will create more problems for us! If on the other hand, we approach him as the Divine in human form, ever gracious and merciful, he will solve all our problems. The innumerable mystics and devotees of कृष्ण over the centuries, are the standing proof of this.

Kṛṣṇamiśra
------------------------------------------
One of the novel methods adopted by the philosophers of the schools of Vedānta was to present their tenets in and through a story or a drama. कृष्णमिश्र, who was probably a recluse living in the 11th century A. D. has done a good job of it in his famous work Prabodha Candrodaya. It is said that he wrote it to convince one of his disciples who had no faith in Vedānta, about the truth and greatness of Advaita Vedānta.
He was closely associated with a king—Kīrtivarma by name—in whose presence the drama was first enacted.
The drama Prabodha Candrodaya has six acts and reflects the whole life of a man with a profound philosophical allegory. It is conceived as a struggle between the two powerful sons—Moha (delusion) and विवेक (discrimination or wisdom)—of the king मनस् (mind), born respectively of his two queens Pravṛtti (worldly life) and निवृत्ति (Monastic life). The drama gives us an ingenious picture of the spiritual struggle of the human मिन्द् in the form of a vivid conflict, wherein the comic, the erotic and the devotional interests play a prominent part. In the final battle between विवेक and मोह, the former wins due to the rise of the मोओन् (candrodaya) of knowledge (prabodha).
Though Advaita Vedānta is eulogised, Viṣṇubhakti or devotion to Lord विष्णु is also advocated as necessary for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
